subject: Recap and next steps: SDK/auth + tool-calling patterns for CloudFin
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Soto <alex@cloudfin.com>
Cc: Aisha Rahman <aisha_rahman@redwood.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 9 Mar 2026 14:05:00 -0700
Subject: Recap and next steps: SDK/auth + tool-calling patterns for CloudFin

Hi Alex — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we keep momentum. Notes below are intentionally prescriptive so Rishi (cc'd) can draft an integration sketch for your architects.

Call highlights / product fit:
- Primary goal: embed transaction-safe, low-latency LLM features into CloudFin's reconciliation workflow (high QPS, strict PII controls).
- Key concerns you raised: auth & keys, routing to on-prem vs hosted, structured outputs for downstream ingestion, and how to wire tool/function calling for bank reconciliation steps (balance check, transaction lookup, exception handling).

Proposed architecture bullets (high level):
- SDK: start with Redwood Node SDK (server-side only) behind a narrow service boundary in your backend. We recommend a service per subsystem (reconciliation-service, metadata-service) that calls Redwood via short-lived auth tokens.
- Auth: support for API keys + optional mTLS for on-prem Dedicated lanes; KMS integration for key rotation; RBAC on tokens scoped by route.
- Routing: policy layer to route reads to hosted models and sensitive flows to your Private deployment (VPC). Failover to a lower-cost variant if Private pool is full.
- Structured output / tool calling: prefer explicit tool definitions with strict JSON schemas for the most sensitive steps (e.g., {"action":"lookup_tx","params":{"tx_id":"string"}}). Use function-calling for deterministic ops and structured output validation for productible ingestion.
- Embeddings/rerankers: embed customer doc corpus nightly (batched), store vectors in your vector DB (we can recommend Faiss/Elastic/kNN). Reranker should be a light model (instruction-following) that re-scores top-N candidate matches returned by the vector DB.

Open questions / asks from you:
1) Do you have a preferred vector DB today?
2) Expected latency SLOs for an interactive reconciliation step?
3) Any compliance constraints preventing sending hashed transaction IDs to hosted environment?

Next steps (proposed):
- Rishi: will produce a one-page integration-pattern doc + example tool definitions and error-handling plan (ETA 48 hours).
- Marissa/Aisha: finalize MAP spreadsheet and send over procurement hints (attached).
- Alex: confirm vector DB and latency SLOs so Rishi can align patterns.

Attachments: MAP-CloudFin-Redwood.xlsx (mutual action plan)

Thanks —
Marissa Cole

Subject: Re: Recap and next steps: SDK/auth + tool-calling patterns for CloudFin

Marissa — really helpful recap, thank you. A few clarifying points from our side: 

1) Vector DB: we currently run an Elastic-based embedding store (in-house). Happy to evaluate Faiss but migrating is non-trivial.
2) Latency SLO: interactive reconciliation must return results within 600ms p95 for the UI flow. Background batch jobs can be relaxed.
3) Compliance: we cannot send raw transaction IDs or PII to any hosted system. Hashing + K-anonymity transformations are acceptable, but we need to validate.

Specific questions about tool/function calling:
- When you say "tool definitions with strict JSON schemas", how do you recommend we model optional vs required params? We have some tools where params are fuzzy (e.g., free-text notes).
- For parallel tools: can multiple tool calls be executed in parallel and then aggregated? What about ordering dependencies (lookup must finish before state-change)?
- Error handling: if a downstream bank API times out while a tool call is in-flight, should Redwood retry or should the client orchestrator handle retries?

I've attached a rough network diagram that shows our hybrid topology (network-diagram.png). Happy to hop on a short call with Rishi if helpful.

Cheers,
Alex Soto
Head of Platform Engineering
CloudFin Solutions

To: Alex Soto <alex@cloudfin.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Aisha Rahman <aisha_rahman@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 11 Mar 2026 09:32:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Recap and next steps: SDK/auth + tool-calling patterns for CloudFin — integration patterns (attached)

Alex / Marissa — thanks. I put together a concise integration-patterns PDF (attached) and pasted the most actionable items below so you can iterate quickly. Happy to take this into a 30-min architecture sync.

1) Tool definition schema (recommended canonical shape)
- Schema URL: https://drive.redwood/integration-samples/tool-schema-v1.json (attachment contains printable copy)
- Minimal example: {"name":"lookup_tx","description":"Fetch transaction by id","params":{"tx_id":{"type":"string","required":true},"include_history":{"type":"boolean","required":false}}}
- Guidance: mark anything PII-sensitive as required and enforce server-side masking. For fuzzy params (free-text notes) model them as optional and treat them as untrusted input (sanitize & length limit).

2) Required vs optional params
- Required: parameters the downstream tool cannot operate without (tx_id, account_id).
- Optional: contextual fields that improve results (notes, user_hint). Use explicit defaults in schema; do not rely on model to fill required fields.

3) Parallel tools and orchestration patterns
- Pattern A (parallel-read then aggregate): execute independent reads in parallel (e.g., balances, ledger snapshot, enrichment) with a bounded concurrency (max 5) and a global timeout (e.g., 300ms). Aggregate results and pass to reranker/decision model.
- Pattern B (ordered with dependency): for operations that mutate state, enforce sequential steps: lookup -> validate -> apply. Use optimistic locking on state-change.
- Implementation note: use request IDs and idempotency tokens for all mutating calls to prevent double-applications on retries.

4) Error handling & retry responsibilities (who does what)
- Redwood's runtime: automatically retries transient infra/hardware errors within tokenized limits (transparent to customer). However, application-level retries (bank API calls, 3rd-party vendors) should be owned by your orchestrator. Reasons: different idempotency guarantees and billing concerns.
- Recommended flow: Redwood returns structured error codes. If a tool call to a bank API times out:
  - Orchestrator: retry with exponential backoff (up to 2 attempts) if the operation is idempotent.
  - If non-idempotent, surface failure to user and create a compensation job.
  - Use a circuit breaker per vendor endpoint (open after N failures for T seconds).

5) Timeouts & SLOs
- For p95 600ms interactive target: aim for 250-300ms budget on model inference and reranking, 150-200ms on vector retrievals/DB, and 50-150ms buffer for network and middleware.
- If your Elastic retrieval is slow, prefetch top candidates asynchronously and cache on the reconciliation-service for hot accounts.

6) Embeddings + reranker (Elastic-specific guidance)
- Keep nightly embedding batches for historical data; use incremental embedding for recent transactions.
- Top-K retrieval from Elastic -> run a light reranker (smaller Llama-family or instruction-tuned opt) hosted on Dedicated with KV cache warmed for common queries.
- Reranker choice: prioritize precision for top-5; use a smaller model (lower latency) and tune for pairwise scoring if possible.

7) Function-calling examples and failure modes
- Example flow: model returns structured call: {"action":"lookup_tx","params":{"tx_id":"abc-123"}}
  - Orchestrator validates schema, performs lookup, returns {"status":"ok","result":{...}} back to model if sequential.
  - For parallel flows, collect results and send aggregated evidence to model for final decision.
- Failure modes: partial results, tool timeouts, invalid schema. Always validate the tool response schema server-side before using. If invalid, reject and surface structured error to the model.

8) Telemetry & observability
- Surface per-call latency, model variant, tool name, and decision outcome. Log request_id, user_id hash, and redaction-level.
- Expose quick traces in Redwood Console for first 30 days of a rollout.

9) Auth & token scope patterns
- Short-lived tokens issued by your auth-service (10–15m) scoped to a route and model; use RBAC claims for read vs write.
- For Private deployment: prefer mTLS + customer-managed KMS; for hosted flows use rotated API keys stored in your KMS and never in plaintext.

10) Quick SDK snippet (Node-style, pseudocode)
- init: const client = new Redwood({auth: getShortLivedToken()});
- tool call: const call = await client.call({model:'redwood-llm-ops',input,tools:['lookup_tx']});
- parallel example (promise.all with timeouts): Promise.race with timeout wrapper + client.call for each read; then aggregate.

Attachments: integration-patterns.pdf (one-page patterns + examples)

If this looks good, we can schedule the 30-min sync to map those patterns to your network diagram and pick explicit model variants for reranker/inference.
